2879.note: Seen today (Waseda repository PDF i14_a4582, waseda.repo.nii.ac.jp/records/34552): a Government Telegraphs form, Motono to 'Okuma Sangi, Yedo', handed in at Nagasaki 7 Nov 1874 (London 6th, 1.38 pm), 'Reply to telegram 3rd instant', then 83 two-digit groups plus 5500 (x4) and 97110000, ending in clear 'above is not in England'. Every group has a red katakana note above it, and these notes match the 1874 table 電信秘號九九格 in i14_a0133 (2-digit = column,row of a 9x9 iroha grid: 14 ニ, 17 ト, 25 カ, 64 ゲ, 73 ブ, 87 君). But the resulting kana stream as I read it (氏 グ ヒ ヲ ブ ナ ヘ 了 ヤ ゴ / ニ ナリ フ グ バ ツ ト 了 ブ ...) does not read as Japanese, and runs like 44 63 71 repeat. So the red notes may be only the code-to-kana step, with a second layer still unread. No verdict until a reader of Japanese checks the red kana: if they make sense, close it as read; if not, it is a strong open lead with the table held.

2065.note: The WVU record answers again (curl, 16 Nov 2026): collection A&M 1841, 'Draft of a telegram sent by Major General George B. McClelland from Clarksburg to General Morris on 30 June 1861, via the Baltimore & Ohio R. R. Telegraph. Part of the message appears to be in code.' One item, 0.01 lin. ft, no digital object. The archive's wording is hedged ('appears to be'), and McClellan's own draft may hold only Stager-style code words for names, so I give no verdict. No printed text was found: a web search and the spirit61.info calendar of McClellan's 1861 papers list a 20 June telegram to Morris and nothing for 30 June. The two archive.org items labelled 'v.2' in the Official Records collection proved to be Series II and III, so OR Ser. I vol. 2 was not checked.
